parts.text: I use awareness to mean bare, non-reflective appearance: blue is just blue. parts.text: I think this non-manifesting awareness should have been “nonmanifesting awarenesses,” strange as that sounds. That missing plural matters. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu opens correctly in The Mind Like Fire Unbound and The Wings to Awakening, saying the mind fabricates the experienced cosmos, including time and the present. But then he still leaves in one copy-pasted line in the singular, “consciousness without feature, without end, luminous all around,” which makes it sound like one single consciousness. He can’t imagine parallel flows as nibbāna, because the suttas say nibbāna lacks “differentiation.”

parts.text: Stream entry’s greatest prize is a “release date”: AN 3.88 allows at most seven more lives before final awakening. There is actually quite a lot of modern academic evidence for rebirth. But who’s going around getting reborn if no permanent self exists? Buddhists don’t imagine any permanent self-essence/soul moving between bodies. Rather, rebirth is seen as a causal process: there is a continuity (often called a “mind-stream”), but there is not a “thing” that’s moving from one life to the next. Craving and clinging lead to becoming, and becoming leads to birth. More like a driverless car. The later Buddhist philosopher Milindapañha compared rebirth to one lamp being used to lighting another.

parts.text: , until I found out the famous stanza I loved comes from the much later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts do give us some very similar kind of symbolism, though. SN 22.95 shows us how form is empty and always transforming, like foam, fleeting feeling is compared to a bubble, perception is only a mirage, and consciousness is basically the best magic trick. And Dhammapada 170 asks us to see the world as a bubble and mirage, so if you put it all together, you can certainly imagine that the basic idea of life being like a dream was originally intended.
